classification_signals: ABSTRACT: 'To present a comprehensive review of the research literature on the effects of the architectural designs of mental health facilities on the users.'

ABSTRACT: 'researchers conducted a systematic search of peer reviewed literature addressing mental health care and architectural design published between 2005 to 2012, as well as a systematic search for academic theses for the period 2000 to 2012.'
Introduction (p. 2): 'The objective of this article is to present an updated review of the literature across health and architecture, but with a specific focus on mental health care and design...'
Methodology (p. 3): 'For this article we combined comprehensive and systematic reviews of the literature on mental health and architecture.'
Methodology (p. 3): 'we utilized selected databases, set dates, and utilized a defined keyword search criteria (see Table 1).'
Methodology (p. 4): 'Once the literature was collated and annotated, we identified key themes (Table 3)...'
title: Stressed Spaces: Mental Health and Architecture

findings.antecedent: Crowding in psychiatric wards
findings.consequent: Risk factors for safety issues (violence, loss of privacy, loss of control)
findings.quote: Crowding appears to be emerging as one of many potential risk factors for safety issues. ...patients lose privacy and also control over their immediate environment.

findings.antecedent: Architectural principles (dedicating space for social interaction, clearly indicating room's intended use, visually distinct areas, colors, materials, lighting to define space, spaces with special meaning)
findings.consequent: Enhanced therapeutic environment
findings.quote: This situation can be reversed by incorpo-rating architectural principles that enhance the therapeutic environment

findings.antecedent: Additional space on acute-care psychiatric ward
findings.consequent: Episodes of aggression
findings.quote: Nijman and Rector's 1999 study that found providing additional space on an acute-care psy-chiatric ward lessened episodes of aggression.

findings.antecedent: Ward environments
findings.consequent: Space occupied by people
findings.quote: Johnstone (2004) notes that people in ward environments occupy 70% less space than did their counterparts of 150 year ago.

findings.antecedent: Unsafe ward environments (violence, aggression, self-harm, absconding, environment-specific issues)
findings.consequent: Mental health notifications
findings.quote: out of 1,367 [statutory] mental health notifications, 89% relate to unsafe ward environments

findings.antecedent: Standardized, single variable-acuity rooms
findings.consequent: Sense of normalcy, control of infection spread
findings.quote: standardized, single variable-acuity rooms mean that patients do not have to be moved when their condition changes, enhancing a sense of normalcy and con-trolling the spread of infection

findings.antecedent: Visually distinct spaces
findings.consequent: Clarity of space function
findings.quote: visually distinct spaces ensure that the function of the space is clear.

findings.antecedent: Lighting
findings.consequent: Accurate performance of visual tasks, reduction of error
findings.quote: lighting enables accurate performance of visual tasks, logically, by reducing error.

findings.antecedent: Daylight and proximity to windows
findings.consequent: Positive mood and perception
findings.quote: positive impacts included daylight and proximity to windows

findings.antecedent: Glare and thermal discomfort
findings.consequent: Negative mood and task performance
findings.quote: negative impact of “glare and thermal discomfort on mood and task performance” were evident.

findings.antecedent: Light exposure (control of circadian system)
findings.consequent: Quality of sleep, enhanced rest-activity patterns (dementia patients)
findings.quote: control of the circadian system, which included a number of ben-efits (e.g., substantial increases in the quality of sleep and enhanced rest-activity patterns in patients with dementia).

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light (2,500 and 10,000 lux, especially in morning)
findings.consequent: Depression, symptoms of seasonal affective disorder (SAD), depressive phase of bipolar disorder
findings.quote: connections between exposure to bright light and depression; symp-toms of seasonal affective disorder (SAD) and the depressive phase of bipolar disorder were diminished

findings.antecedent: Exposure to light
findings.consequent: Length of depressed patients' stays in hospital
findings.quote: documenting a connection between exposure to light and the length of depressed patients' stays in the hospital.

findings.antecedent: Increased intensity of sunlight (patients on bright side of hospital unit)
findings.consequent: Perceived stress, pain, pain medication costs
findings.quote: patients exposed to an increased intensity of sunlight experienced less perceived stress, marginally less pain, and had 21% less pain medication costs

findings.antecedent: Natural light (vs. artificial lighting)
findings.consequent: Human chronobiology (SAD, sleep disorders, work disruptions)
findings.quote: different effects of natural versus artificial lighting on patients, specifically in the areas of illuminance, uniformity, diffusion, color, and UV radiation. These, in turn, affect human chronobiology, contributing to, for example, seasonal affective disorder (SAD), sleep disorders, and work disruptions.

findings.antecedent: Natural circadian rhythm of light
findings.consequent: Melatonin production, biochemical and hormonal body rhythms
findings.quote: the natural circadian rhythm of light regulates melatonin production, influencing biochemical and hormonal body rhythms.

findings.antecedent: Natural light (for eating disorder patients who cannot use food to regulate body)
findings.consequent: Circadian rhythms
findings.quote: natural light is a key design consideration.

findings.antecedent: Lighting
findings.consequent: Endocrine systems, Vitamin D production
findings.quote: lighting is important for more than just vision, affecting endocrine systems and producing Vitamin D

findings.antecedent: Daylight and routine activities outdoors
findings.consequent: Sensory stimulation, interaction with nature, beneficial effect on Alzheimer's patients
findings.quote: The positive associations of daylight and routine activities outdoors with sensory stimulation and interaction with nature was seen to have a beneficial effect on patients suf-fering from Alzheimer's

findings.antecedent: Brightly lit rooms (vs. dimly lit rooms)
findings.consequent: Length of stay in psychiatric hospital
findings.quote: patients in brightly lit rooms stayed on average 16.9 days versus19.5 days for those in dimly lit rooms, a difference of nearly 3 days (2.6 days difference).

findings.antecedent: Natural light
findings.consequent: Circadian system control, reduced depression, decreased length of stay, improved sleep, lessened agitation, eased pain, easier adaptation to night-shift work
findings.quote: Commonalities for all publications related to light include the importance of controlling the circadian system. Natural circadian rhythms regulate melatonin production, which influences biochemical and hormonal body rhythms, which have the following effects upon mental health: reduced depression, decreased length of stay, improved sleep and circadian rhythm, lessened agitation, eased pain, and easier adaptation to night-shift work.

findings.antecedent: Lack of natural lighting
findings.consequent: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD), changes to hormonal body rhythms, glare and flicker, work disruptions, increased staff stress, decreased staff satisfaction
findings.quote: a lack of natural lighting can cause seasonal affective disorder (SAD), changes to hormonal body rhythms, glare and flicker, work disruptions, increased staff stress, and decreased staff satisfaction

findings.antecedent: Client-centered design (residential addiction and mental health facilities)
findings.consequent: Comfort, abundance of natural light, freedom, reduced stigma, enhanced sense of well-being (positive outcomes for clients)
findings.quote: Positive outcomes and perceptions from the focus groups made repeated reference to comfort, abundance of natural light, freedom, reduced stigma with new spatial designs that mimicked a “normal” community setting and an enhanced sense of well-being

findings.antecedent: Client-centered design (residential addiction and mental health facilities)
findings.consequent: Limited staff space, difficulty sharing confidential information, reduced sightlines to clients (negative outcomes for staff)
findings.quote: negative outcomes and perceptions around limited staff space and the ability to share confidential information, and staff concerns due to reduced sightlines to clients

findings.antecedent: Salutogenic architectural design (perceptual cues, clear textures/objects/lines, familiar environment, safe/cozy home, minimal noise, access to nature/pets, family/friends communication, sensory gratification)
findings.consequent: Fortified sense of coherence, stabilized comprehension/delusions, rehabilitation, positive mental health outcomes
findings.quote: the environment should ensure that perceptual cues are present to assist perceptual processes; clear textures, objects and lines should prevent the possibility of perceptual distortion and ambiguity. ...the environment should be familiar to psychotic patients as this helps stabilize both comprehension and delusions. ...access to nature, pets, and supported communication with family and friends is essential to rehabilitation. To this end, environmental stimu-lation should provide sensory gratification.

findings.antecedent: Salutogenic approach (control over environment, enriching environment with complexity/order/aesthetics, allowing personal items/pets, stimulating milieu)
findings.consequent: Meaningfulness for patients
findings.quote: it is important to allow patients to control their environment though meaningfulness. This goal can be attained by 'enriching the environment with complexity, order and aesthetic considerations'; allowing pets and personal items on the premises; and providing a stimulating milieu.

findings.antecedent: Architectural aspects of healing environments (views to outside/nature images, adequately sized bathrooms, extra seating, reduced noise, lighting options, comfortable room temperatures, aesthetics)
findings.consequent: Optimally restful patient environment
findings.quote: architectural aspects of healing environ-ments include those elements that create an optimally restful patient environ-ment.

findings.antecedent: Architectural design for staff (work flow, safety features, visual access to patients, security designs, respite rooms)
findings.consequent: Reduced employee injuries, protection from hostile visitors, staff stress reduction
findings.quote: for 'staff, designs should address: the work flow process of caregiving... safety features... visual access of patients... security designs... and staff stress reduction with the design of respite rooms'

findings.antecedent: Psychiatric hospital design (patient-centered design, ambient features, architectural features, social features, nursing station design, single rooms, private visiting areas, gardens, nature views, flexible spatial design, staff lounges/gardens)
findings.consequent: Enhanced privacy, intimacy, family participation, group activities, positive distractions, minimal institutional connotations, calming (blue tones), staff communication, job satisfaction
findings.quote: Karlin and Zeiss (2006) reviewed environmental and therapeutic issues in psy-chiatric hospital design... recommended the enhanced privacy associated with single rooms and private visiting areas that facilitate intimacy... gardens and views of nature serve as positive distractions.

findings.antecedent: Psychiatric hospital design (no overcrowding, variety of spaces for social interaction, classical daylight, fresh air, openness of design, meticulous care of buildings/grounds, easy observation of patients, segregated staff areas)
findings.consequent: Humane/efficient containment, reduced psychopathology, reduced vandalism, staff engagement with patients
findings.quote: design elements included no overcrowding... provision of a variety of spaces that supported social interaction; an abundance of “classical" daylight and fresh air; openness of design to encourage staff to leave the nursing station... easy observation of patients; and segregation of staff work and rest areas.

findings.antecedent: Psychiatric intensive care unit design (ground floor access to enclosed gardens, separate entrance, wide corridors, good-sized quiet recreation room, avoidance of numerous corners/corridors, disturbance buttons, louver-type observation panels, vandal-proof light fittings, homely fixtures/fittings)
findings.consequent: Improved patient care, homely environment
findings.quote: Dix and Williams (1996) made recommendations for the design of psychiatric intensive care units, suggesting that the sites/wards should be on the ground floor with access to enclosed gardens... and also advocated fixtures and fittings that provide a homely environment.

findings.antecedent: Blues (color)
findings.consequent: Aggressive individuals
findings.quote: blues have been indicated to subdue aggressive individuals

findings.antecedent: Visual monotony
findings.consequent: Physiological and emotional stress
findings.quote: visual monotony can contribute to physiological and emotional stress

findings.antecedent: Surfaces (tactile experience)
findings.consequent: Patients' recovery, re-engagement with materiality of the world
findings.quote: surfaces help to “re-engage with the materiality of the world"

findings.antecedent: Perceptual confusion (e.g., wood-grain finish on metal door)
findings.consequent: Inaccurate sensory information
findings.quote: perceptual confusion should be avoided (e.g., a wood-grain finish on a metal door would give inaccurate sen-sory information because a metal door will be heavier and colder than would be expected with a real wooden door).

findings.antecedent: Excessive noise
findings.consequent: Increased heart rate, blood pressure, respiration, blood cholesterol
findings.quote: excessive noise has implications for increased heart rate, blood pressure, respiration, and blood cholesterol

findings.antecedent: Hard materials
findings.consequent: Noise absorption
findings.quote: hard materials absorb less noise.

findings.antecedent: Pleasant smells
findings.consequent: Relaxed muscles, aid concentration, endorphin production, decreased heart rate, reduced anesthetic administered during surgery
findings.quote: smell can relax muscles and aid concentration; pleasant smells help produce endorphins and can decrease heart rate. Further, they noted the hypothesis that pleasant smells can reduce the amount of anesthetic administered during surgery

findings.antecedent: Lack of windows and connection to outside world
findings.consequent: Stress and depression
findings.quote: a lack of windows and connection to the outside world can heighten stress and depression.

findings.antecedent: Therapeutic milieu design (light, adequate personal/communal/work space, home-like comfort, access to gardens)
findings.consequent: Positive mental health outcomes
findings.quote: the commonalities across the literature on providing a therapeutic milieu through the design of facilities for mental health care focus on the ele-ments of light; adequate personal, communal, and work space; home-like com-fort; and access to gardens.

findings.antecedent: Healing gardens (absence of harsh noises/unwanted demands, knowledge of healing plants)
findings.consequent: Health (physical, mental, social continua)
findings.quote: healing gardens... are allied with a broad conception of health, one that recognizes that a person can move between greater and lesser degrees of health along diverse physical, mental and social continua

findings.antecedent: Availability of outside space (for nurses)
findings.consequent: Importance for workday, importance for co-workers
findings.quote: the availability of an outside space was important to those nurses surveyed; 88% said it was important to get outside during their workday and nearly all of the participants felt it was import-ant for their co-workers to get outside.

findings.antecedent: Outdoor spaces (sitting, walking, eating, close to nature, sunshine, fresh air, social interaction)
findings.consequent: Nurse well-being, stress relief
findings.quote: Favorite activities included sitting (25%), walking (21%), and eating (10%). Nine percent expressed the need to be close to nature and get some sunshine and fresh air, while others went out to be social

findings.antecedent: Moral therapy (18th/19th century asylums, carefully designed environment, viewing landscape from inside)
findings.consequent: Positive effects on patients, reduced physical restraints
findings.quote: It was believed that viewing the landscape had positive effects on the patients and therefore buildings were designed so the landscape could be viewed from inside the building as well.

findings.antecedent: Gardens (in post-asylum age mental health care)
findings.consequent: Attachment, therapeutic benefits (for long-term patients)
findings.quote: long-term patients were known to return to the asylums in which they were housed in order to walk in the gardens because of an attachment to and their positive associations with the therapeutic benefits of such places

findings.antecedent: Nature (as a restorative element, integrated framework of directed attention, attention restoration theory)
findings.consequent: Restorative experience, less effort than 'civilized' environment, longer term benefits, new initiatives
findings.quote: being in nature requires less effort than being in a “civilized” environment; that intervention measures suggest that the use of nature as a restorative method have longer term benefits

findings.antecedent: Therapeutic gardens (Alzheimer's facility)
findings.consequent: Visitors feeling more relaxed, calmer, refreshed
findings.quote: The interview data revealed that 75% of visitors reported feeling more relaxed and calmer and 25% felt refreshed.

findings.antecedent: Gardens (designed for safety, reflection, relaxation, socialization, gardening hobby)
findings.consequent: Aims met (except for gardening hobby due to lack of space)
findings.quote: 80% of respondents said the aims of the gardens were met, except for providing a place for people to maintain a gardening hobby, as the gardens were already fully planted with no free space

findings.antecedent: Single bed rooms
findings.consequent: Patient privacy, confidentiality, communication
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 17
findings.quote: patient privacy and confidentiality as well as communication improves with single bed rooms

findings.antecedent: Day and appropriate lighting
findings.consequent: Positive health outcomes (14 of 16 listed)
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 17
findings.quote: day and appropriate lighting contributed posi-tively to 14 of the 16 health outcomes listed

findings.antecedent: Nature views
findings.consequent: Reduced pain, stress, positive health outcomes (5 others)
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 17
findings.quote: nature views contributes signifi-cantly to reduced pain and stress and also to five other health outcomes

findings.antecedent: Built environment (as source of stress, influence on social networks/support, symbolic effects/social labeling, planning process)
findings.consequent: Cause-and-effect associations with mental health
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 17
findings.quote: Halpern's approach of cause-and-effect associations of the built environment according to the following four categories: as a source of stress; as an influence over social networks and support; through symbolic effects and social labeling; and through the action of the (building) planning process itself.

findings.antecedent: Environment designed to change for and with patient's sensory and perceptual abilities
findings.consequent: Positive outcomes
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 18
findings.quote: if the environment can be designed to change for and with the patient's sensory and perceptual abilities, positive out-comes could result.

findings.antecedent: Sensory environment (smells, noise, temperature, environmental complexity, fresh air/ventilation, color, nature, art/aesthetics, entertainment)
findings.consequent: Patient preferences in healthcare setting
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 18
findings.quote: Schweitzer et al. presented the existing research in terms of physical parameters, and as includ-ing the following preferences in a healthcare setting: smells, noise, temperature, environmental complexity, fresh air and ventilation, color, nature, art/aesthetics and entertainment, and nursing stations.

findings.antecedent: Pleasing aromas
findings.consequent: Reduced blood pressure, slow respiration, lower pain perception levels
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 18
findings.quote: pleasing aromas may reduce blood pressure, slow respira-tion, and lower pain perception levels

findings.antecedent: Unpleasant odors
findings.consequent: Anxiety, fear, stress
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: unpleasant odors stimulate anxiety, fear, and stress.

findings.antecedent: Excessive noise
findings.consequent: Patients' length of stay, interruption of sleep, increased stress
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: excessive noise increases patients' length of stay as well as causing interruption of sleep and increased stress

findings.antecedent: Environments with greater complexity
findings.consequent: Greater cognitive functioning, beneficial physical activity (elderly)
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: environments with greater complexity correlate with greater cognitive functioning and beneficial physical activity in the elderly

findings.antecedent: Sensory variation in ambient conditions (between spaces and over time)
findings.consequent: Building occupants' preference
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: sensory varia-tion in ambient conditions between spaces and over time is preferred by building occupants.

findings.antecedent: Lack of a window
findings.consequent: Reduced positive stimulation, aggravated negative effects of sensory deprivation
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: lack of a window, which may have a negative effect by reducing positive stimulation and aggravating the negative effects of sensory deprivation

findings.antecedent: Access to views of nature (with gardens, through windows, in artwork)
findings.consequent: Reduced stress
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: access to views of nature with gardens, through windows and in artwork, can reduce stress

findings.antecedent: Patients residing in units without windows
findings.consequent: Symptoms of depression
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: patients residing in units without windows developed more symptoms of depression.

findings.antecedent: Experiencing nature
findings.consequent: Lowered stress, muscle tension, fewer incidences of violence
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: lowered stress and muscle tension”... and fewer incidences of violence.

findings.antecedent: Indoor plants
findings.consequent: Beneficial effects
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: Indoor plants were also shown to be beneficial.

findings.antecedent: Visual art (nature images, positive facial expressions, depiction of caring relationships)
findings.consequent: Preference
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: a preference was shown for visual art encompassing nature images, positive facial expressions, and depiction of caring relationships

findings.antecedent: Ambiguous or abstract imagery (visual art)
findings.consequent: Negative outcomes
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: ambiguous or abstract imagery was shown to have nega-tive outcomes.

findings.antecedent: Music, positive distractions (humor, entertainment)
findings.consequent: Greater optimism, socialization, cooperation, decreased dependence on medication
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: positive effect of music on health and also positive distractions such as humor and entertainment, which may lead to greater optimism, socialization, coopera-tion, and decreased dependence on medication.

findings.antecedent: Perceptual cues
findings.consequent: Assisted perceptual processes, avoided confusion
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: Perceptual cues assist the perceptual processes, help avoid confusion.

findings.antecedent: Environment enriched with complexity, order, aesthetic considerations
findings.consequent: Beneficial outcomes
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: Enriching the environment with complexity, order, and aesthetic consid-erations is beneficial.

findings.antecedent: Access to nature
findings.consequent: Positive mental health outcomes, added complexity and stimulation
findings.source: Impact of Architecture on Health Outcomes, p. 19
findings.quote: Access to nature can have positive mental health outcomes and add com-plexity and stimulation.

findings.antecedent: Interior design (colorful wallpaper, paintings, lowered ceilings, multiple lighting spots, curtains, wardrobes, chairs, flowers, personal items, Italian ceramic tile bathroom)
findings.consequent: Negative effects, length of patient stay, vandalism
findings.quote: The findings included “no negative effects of changing to a more pleasant and home-like environment” (p. 22); non-significant tendency toward symptom amelioration in the traditional wing; creating a pleasant environment does not generally increase length of patient stay; and there was a “complete lack of vandalism" (p. 23) on the new side.

findings.antecedent: Interior design and furnishing (like an ordinary home)
findings.consequent: Comparable treatment outcomes (to dismal interior), positive effects on patient well-being (especially women)
findings.quote: interior and furnishing like an ordinary home created an environment with comparable treatment outcomes to the traditional dismal interior, and had positive effects on many patients' well-being, at least among the women

findings.antecedent: Wayfinding design (distinct landmarks, appropriate signage, legible text, high contrast, graphic images, color coding, clustered directories, 'You Are Here' designations)
findings.consequent: Better wayfinding (for people with disabilities)
findings.quote: Salmi's (2008) comments on wayfinding for people with disabilities... threw light on universal applications for developing better wayfinding in interior design.

findings.antecedent: Interior decorating changes (color schemes, indoor plants, new furniture, bathroom renovations, increased light)
findings.consequent: Decreased stereotypic behavior (patients), improved staff morale
findings.quote: sufficient data to indi-cate a decrease in stereotypic behavior among patients and improved staff morale after elements such as wallpaper, live plants, increased light, colored walls, and upholstered furniture replaced the previous spaces

findings.antecedent: Depressing hospital environments
findings.consequent: Regression, loss of control, intimidation (for psychiatric patients and families)
findings.quote: depressing environments convey regression and loss of control and present as intimidating for patients and families.

findings.antecedent: Noisy conditions with poor lighting (for staff in PGUs)
findings.consequent: Likelihood of being assaulted
findings.quote: staff working in noisy conditions with poor lighting were more likely to be assaulted

findings.antecedent: Ward environments
findings.consequent: Patients' experiences (loss of self-esteem, intensified psychiatric symptoms, reduced participation in care, 'sanctuary harm')
findings.quote: loss of self-esteem, patients' sense of self-worth, inten-sified psychiatric symptoms, and a reduction in patient's participation in their care may be caused by “sanctuary harm”

findings.antecedent: Optimal physical environment design (patient/staff safety, physical health, productive ward, PICU/HDU access, space for garden/quiet/seclusion/activity, separate bedrooms with observation panels/two-way doors/dimmer lights/safe fixtures/alarms, secure/structured/minimal stimulation/supportive environment, observation-facilitating design, high nurse-to-patient ratios, limited restraints/seclusion, segregation for cognitively impaired, separate male/female sections, direct outdoor access, clear area indications, optimized nurses' station for sightlines, locked doors, external visibility/public transportation access)
findings.consequent: Optimal outcomes for psychogeriatric units
findings.quote: Dohrohot-off and Llewellyn Jones make the following recommendations for designing the optimal physical environment

findings.antecedent: Deinstitutionalizing features (separate living/treatment areas, elimination of echoing corridors/reverberant spaces, residential features like laundry/kitchens, design solutions encouraging social interactions like ward kitchen/open nursing station/dayroom module)
findings.consequent: Reduced psychopathology (younger patients), social interactions
findings.quote: design should incorporate deinstitutionalizing features such as: Separate living and treatment areas. The elimination of long echoing corridors and highly reverberant spaces. Residential features such as a laundry and galley kitchens. Reduced psychopathology among younger patients facilitated by design solutions that encouraged social interactions

findings.antecedent: SCU design (clearly colored wayfinding, names on doors, photos of family, separate activity areas, secure exits/closets, visual tapes across glass, appropriate sound proofing, nature, natural light, recreational activities, personal/gendered spaces)
findings.consequent: Benefits of group living (dementia patients), reduced psychotropic drugs, decline in behavioral disturbance, beneficial for staff/patients
findings.quote: Their findings can be summarized as the benefits of group living for patients with dementia; the disorienting problems with changes to their environment; the benefit of reduced use of psychotropic drugs and a decline in behavioral disturbance in Secure Care Unit (SCU) design that showed clearly colored wayfinding... and other aspects such as the benefits of nature and natural light... were shown to be beneficial to both staff and patients.

findings.antecedent: Environmental alteration (psychiatric ward redesign)
findings.consequent: Changes in social behavior, altered spatial distribution of behavior, reduced psychopathology
findings.quote: They posited four psy-choenvironmental hypotheses for evaluation: 1. Environmental alteration correlates with changes in social behavior. 2. Environmental alteration correlates with altered spatial distribution of behavior. 3. Environmental alteration correlates with reduced psychopathology.

findings.antecedent: Psychiatric ward redesign (psychoenvironmental principles)
findings.consequent: Positive clinical outcomes (limited), reduced length of stay (not substantially)
findings.quote: Their conclusions were positive in terms of clinical outcomes but limited; the authors noted that length of stay was not reduced substantially by the redesign

findings.antecedent: Serious game intervention (to engage low secure service users in design/refurbishment)
findings.consequent: Overwhelmingly positive feedback, successful collaborative dialogue, improved information gathering (vs. traditional consultation)
findings.quote: Feedback from participants was overwhelmingly posi-tive. The use of the serious game format has potential for mental health services to successfully engage service users in collaborative dialogue... the resulting information from the game was better.

findings.antecedent: Nursing station design (physical barriers)
findings.consequent: Patients' perception of off-limits work area, impeded interactions
findings.quote: The physical barriers used in the design of nursing stations rein-force the idea that they are off-limits to patients and impede the development of interactions.

findings.antecedent: Redesigns including more private areas for nurses
findings.consequent: Positive nurse-patient interactions
findings.quote: positive nurse-patient interactions “increased dra-matically" after redesigns that "include more private areas for nurses”

findings.antecedent: Nursing station design (combined intense administrative activity with patient interaction)
findings.consequent: Inadequate patient-staff communication
findings.quote: the design of the nursing station combined intense administrative activity with patient interaction with the result inade-quate patient-staff communication.

findings.antecedent: Optimal nursing station design (appropriate seating, stimulants, acoustics, size for function, therapy spaces close to nurses' stations, patient boundary, high visibility)
findings.consequent: Improved staff/patient interaction, safety
findings.quote: the optimal design of the nursing station needed to incorporate appropriate seating, stimulants, acoustics, and size to suit the intended function of the space and to place thera-py spaces close to nurse stations. A sense of boundary to the patient is necessary but there still needs to be high visibility.

findings.antecedent: Removal of glass partitions from psychiatric unit nursing stations
findings.consequent: Significant positive psychological, behavioral, social effects, reduced patient requests, reduced negative beliefs, improved ward milieu, improved patient-staff communication
findings.quote: significant positive psychological, behavioral, and social effects after the removal of glass partitions from psychiatric unit nursing stations. Patient requests of nurs-es at nursing stations were dramatically reduced, as were the negative beliefs of those patients, and improvements in ward milieu and patient-staff communica-tion were also noted

findings.antecedent: Open nursing stations
findings.consequent: Patient abuse (concerns of increased access to nurses)
findings.quote: available reports of experiences with open nursing stations do not support concerns of patient abuse of increased access to nurses

findings.antecedent: Contiguous, secure, closed nursing stations (to patients)
findings.consequent: Confidentiality of patient records
findings.quote: Contiguous, secure, closed to patients, is recommended to maintain confidentiality of patient records

findings.antecedent: Closed nursing stations (pre-psychoactive medications)
findings.consequent: Perception of staff inaccessibility, staff not welcoming patients/visitors
findings.quote: closed nursing stations were the norm, but they fostered a perception that the staff members were inaccessible and welcomed neither patients nor visitors to their environs.

findings.antecedent: Large centralized nursing stations (separated by half-walls/glass partitions, distant from patient rooms)
findings.consequent: Staff distance from patients, message of staff busyness/inaccessibility
findings.quote: large centralized nursing stations separated from patients by half-walls or glass partitions that are located some distance from the rooms of the patients “clearly distance staff members from patients, sending the message that they are busy and inaccessible”

findings.antecedent: Decentralized nursing work station (small, open, outside clusters of 4-6 patient rooms, main nursing station completely open to patients)
findings.consequent: Healing as collaborative process (not exclusive to professionals)
findings.quote: a decentralized nursing work station that is small, open and located outside clusters of 4–6 patient rooms, with the main nursing station completely open to patients, suggest[s] that healing is a collaborative pro-cess and not something exclusively under the purview of ‘professionals”

findings.antecedent: Nursing stations (discreet/separate spaces for staff relaxation/administrative tasks, open areas for patient/staff interaction)
findings.consequent: Improved staff well-being, improved patient/staff interaction, welcoming environment
findings.quote: The commonalities for all publications which relate to nursing stations include the need for discreet and separate spaces for nurses and other staff to relax and also for spaces away from patients where they can attend to administrative tasks. In addition, open areas are necessary to encourage interactions between patients and staff because closed nursing stations often convey an image of staff inacces-sibility and are not welcoming to patients and visitors.

findings.antecedent: Traditional approach to mental health treatment ('rehabilitation and acute psychiatry as dichotomous')
findings.consequent: Questioned effectiveness
findings.quote: The professionals at the Centre had come to question their traditional approach to mental health treat-ment, 'rehabilitation and acute psychiatry were perceived as dichotomous'

findings.antecedent: New 'phase of illness' model of care (integrating early intervention, balancing risk/vulnerability with patient experience/recovery, acknowledging disability levels, not targeting rehabilitation only for severe disability)
findings.consequent: Improved services responsive to patient illness phases
findings.quote: Their main points included attempts to integrate 'early intervention' approaches into the philosophy of a large insti-tution to provide services responsive to the different phases of a patient's illness

findings.antecedent: Current models of mental health care facilities (hospitals, independent living, group homes)
findings.consequent: Insufficient continuum of care, disregard for therapeutic qualities, lack of connection to therapy, isolation
findings.quote: problems with current models of mental health care facilities... include being insufficient as a continuum of care model for mentally ill patients; hospitals disregard therapeutic qualities... group homes can be problematic as they can act as small isolated islands within the community.

findings.antecedent: Architecture balancing supervision, treatment, freedom, community integration (design principles: connection with community/retreat, retail as buffer, integrated building form, interactive wayfinding, multiple levels of interaction)
findings.consequent: Improved mental health care
findings.quote: Costello's (2007) thesis advocated for an architecture that balances supervision, treatment, freedom, and community integration... Key design principles recommended were: Balance between connection with the community and retreat. Retail as a buffer between life in the facility and life in the larger community. Integrated building form... Interactive wayfinding. Facility design should support multiple levels of interaction.

findings.antecedent: Bio-psycho-social approach (psychological therapy, spirituality, social networking, group/family therapy, personal visual elements, ability to withdraw)
findings.consequent: Holistic patient treatment, grounded sense of self, self-discovery
findings.quote: Fitzpatrick's (2007) study addressed mental health care from a bio-psycho-social perspective, one that aims to treat the patient holistically... personal visual elements may ground a person's sense of self, and a sense of self can add to the experience of space. In addition, being able to with-draw is important as well as aiding a person with self discovery.

findings.antecedent: Financial incentives (U.S. Medicaid program)
findings.consequent: Length of stay of psychiatric patients
findings.quote: Frank and Lave (1986) provided an analysis that showed that the treat-ment of psychiatric patients and their length of stay responds strongly to finan-cial incentives.

findings.antecedent: Designated ward for homeless mentally ill
findings.consequent: Housing stability, engagement with services, medication non-compliance
findings.quote: those admitted were no more likely to be discharged or to move on to or remain in stable housing than were those in the control group... However, there was an improvement seen in engagement with services for those who were admitted as well as diminished issues with medication non-compliance.

findings.antecedent: Art interventions
findings.consequent: Depression, anxiety
findings.quote: depression and anxiety were respec-tively 34% and 20% lower where intervention had taken place than with groups not exposed to arts”

findings.antecedent: Abstract art (vs. realistic landscape art)
findings.consequent: PRN medication dispensed for anxiety and agitation
findings.quote: The results did indeed show a substantial effect of the nature of the displayed art work on the amount of PRN medication dispensed for anxiety and agitation, being significantly higher when abstract art was featured than when the patients viewed a realistic landscape.

findings.antecedent: Realistic art with nature content (vs. stylized or abstract images)
findings.consequent: Hospital in-patients' preference
findings.quote: Hospital in-patients con-sistently preferred images of realistic art with nature content over images that were stylized or abstract”

findings.antecedent: Design for adolescents (calm down spaces with lifelike imagery, cool colors, increased daylight, varied seating options)
findings.consequent: Met needs of adolescents
findings.quote: Their suggestions, which included “calm down” spaces with in-depth, lifelike imagery; the use of cool colors (blue and purple); increased daylight; and varied seating options... coincided with features suggested by previous EBD research.

findings.antecedent: Adolescent hospitalization
findings.consequent: Importance of access to television (97%), music (96%), telephone (95%)
findings.quote: According to the majority of the young participants, access to a television (97%), music (96%), and a telephone (95%) was of utmost importance.

findings.antecedent: Attention distraction (via television, music, conversations with friends)
findings.consequent: Coping measure in stressful situations (for young people)
findings.quote: the most common coping measure in stressful situations is attention distraction, which can be provided easily by television, music, and conversations with friends.

findings.antecedent: Spaces beyond rooms (area to visit friends, gym/exercise room, accessible kitchen)
findings.consequent: High priority for adolescents
findings.quote: an area in which to visit with friends was of a high priority; 'a gym or exer-cise room to work out in was selected by 82% of participants, and an accessible kitchen was selected by 79% of participants'

findings.antecedent: Adolescent privacy needs (private bathrooms, single rooms, comfortable full-coverage pajamas)
findings.consequent: Expression of identity
findings.quote: the specific developmental traits of ado-lescents seem to call for distinct amenities, such as private bathrooms, single rooms, and comfortable full-coverage pajamas, to provide for the expression of identity

findings.antecedent: Views from windows (medium vegetation, variety of plants/trees/bushes/shrubs/fruits/flowers/vegetables/greens, body of water, houses)
findings.consequent: Adolescents' preferences (dually diagnosed)
findings.quote: medium veg-etation was preferred over dense or sparse vegetation; they wanted variety— plants, trees, bushes, shrubs, vegetation with fruits, flowers, vegetables, and greens; some form of body of water was a favorite, with a pool the most preferred choice; 'houses' were the most preferred kind of building

findings.antecedent: Equal proportions of vegetation and buildings (in window views)
findings.consequent: Adolescents' preference (dually diagnosed)
findings.quote: Almost two-thirds (62.2%) of participants wanted equal proportions of vegetation and buildings.

findings.antecedent: Forensic psychiatric hospital design (ambience, comfortable domestic scale, good lighting, bright colors, subdivided spaces, safe environment, privacy, observability, noise buffering, smaller social units)
findings.consequent: Acquisition of skills, reduced stressors, reasonable therapeutic milieu, freedom for patients
findings.quote: design considerations should include ambience and a comfortable domestic scale, the use of good lighting, bright colors and subdivided spaces, and a safe environment that promotes both pri-vacy and observability and fosters the acquisition of skills. ...anything that can be done to buffer excessive noise would be very helpful. ...best design would offer “a compromise between staff efficiency and a reasonable therapeutic milieu;” it was believed that this could be “achieved with relatively smaller social units” that afforded a reasonable degree of freedom to the patients

findings.antecedent: Building designs with problems (in secure facilities)
findings.consequent: Security breaches, greater number of escapes
findings.quote: security breaches and building design correlated, in that units with design problems are units that experience a greater number of escapes

findings.antecedent: Higher garden fence (in secure facilities)
findings.consequent: Escapes
findings.quote: escapes becomes much less likely the higher the garden fence.

findings.antecedent: Design features for security without compromising patient care (secure bedrooms overlooking inner courtyard, climb-proof courtyard coverings, double overhand fencing, CCTV, airlocks/alarms on exit doors, secure window fittings)
findings.consequent: Enhanced security
findings.quote: Design features that add security without compromis-ing patient care include secure bedrooms overlooking an inner courtyard, any covering of that courtyard modified by a feature that cannot be climbed, fencing with a double overhand, the installation of closed circuit television, airlocks and alarms on exit doors, and new and secure window fittings.

findings.antecedent: Architectural design of psychiatric units (demarcated spaces for activities, extra space)
findings.consequent: Positive mental health outcomes
findings.quote: This has important impli-cations for the architectural design of psychiatric units, including the impor-tance of demarcated spaces for particular activities and extra space provided where possible.

findings.antecedent: Light (natural and artificial)
findings.consequent: Circadian system control, reduced depression, agitation, improved sleep, eased pain
findings.quote: The pri-mary findings here were the importance of light for controlling the circadian system thus reducing depression, agitation, sleep, eating patterns and also easing pain in some instances.

findings.antecedent: Gardens and contact with nature
findings.consequent: Renewal/restoration of attention, stress relief, social aspects
findings.quote: The fourth theme of gardens is revealed as extremely important for both patients and staff for renew-al/restoration of attention, stress relief, and for its social aspects, with evidenced-based research showing high percentages to support this

findings.antecedent: Architecture (complexity, order, aesthetic considerations, perceptual cues, access to nature, sensory/salutogenic considerations)
findings.consequent: Enriched environment, avoided confusion, positive mental health outcomes, privacy, single bedrooms
findings.quote: architecture can enrich the envi-ronment with complexity, order, and aesthetic considerations offering perceptual cues to assist and avoid confusion. Access to nature and sensory/salutogenic con-siderations... as is the need for privacy and a preference of single bedrooms.

findings.antecedent: Interior design (furnishings, color, wayfinding, cognitive mapping, spatial organization, patient room type)
findings.consequent: Clear visual communication, home-like environment
findings.quote: The sixth theme of interior design... shows the need for clear visual communication balanced with a home-like environment

findings.antecedent: Psychogeriatric design (quiet spaces, gardens, deinstitutionalizing features, social interactions)
findings.consequent: Reduced dementia, violence, trauma
findings.quote: The seventh theme is that of psychogeriatric considerations... highlight the need for quiet spaces and gardens, with an emphasis on deinstitutionalizing design fea-tures to encourage social interactions

findings.antecedent: Nurse-only and patient-only spaces (in nursing stations)
findings.consequent: Beneficial outcomes for both groups
findings.quote: nurse-only and patient-only spaces found to be beneficial to both groups.

findings.antecedent: Closed nursing stations
findings.consequent: Image of staff inaccessibility to patients and visitors
findings.quote: Closed nursing stations often convey an image of staff inaccessibility to patients and visitors

findings.antecedent: Model of care (bio-psycho-social approach, personal visual elements, environmental context, psychological/social therapy, interactions)
findings.consequent: Holistic patient treatment, balance between drug-therapy and other therapies
findings.quote: The literature shows the need for a balance between drug-therapy, environmental context and psychological and social therapy and interactions

findings.antecedent: Exposure to arts
findings.consequent: Depression, anxiety
findings.quote: depression and anxiety were 34% and 20% lower, respectively, in contexts where patients were exposed to arts.

findings.antecedent: Design for adolescent mental health patient (connectedness to outside world, family-centered care, visual preferences for medium density gardens with water, access to personal items/movies/private bathrooms)
findings.consequent: Improved mental health outcomes
findings.quote: highlights the need for maintaining connectedness to the outside world, including family-centered care; the role of visual preferences, including medi-um density gardens with water; as well as the need to keep personal items, have access to movies, and have private bathrooms

findings.antecedent: Forensic psychiatric facility design (safety, privacy, pleasant domestic atmosphere, natural light, ample space)
findings.consequent: Improved patient outcomes, reduced escapes
findings.quote: The literature emphasizes a pleasant domes-tic atmosphere that is well-lit with natural light and provides ample space for patients

limitations: Only 25 out of 165 research articles generated evidence-based numerical data, indicating a scarcity of quantitative evidence (p. 3).

There is a lack of reliable post-occupancy evaluations (POEs) of mental health facilities, potentially due to ethical protocols, concerns with qualitative methods on vulnerable populations, cost, fear of negative outcomes, perceived uniqueness of buildings, and difficulties in drawing conclusions amid many variables (p. 3, 24).
Many studies on psychogeriatric unit design are based on opinion, anecdote, or observational studies, with few good quality randomized controlled studies (p. 22).
Small sample sizes are common in studies on design and dementia, making it difficult to detect significant results (p. 23, 30).
Interdisciplinary research in healthcare design faces barriers due to different disciplinary cultures, professional languages, and institutional policies regarding publication and promotion (p. 24).
There are few studies that directly examine arts interventions, and a notable absence of evidence-based studies in this area (p. 30).
Differing perspectives among various stakeholders in mental health care regarding art present challenges for integrated approaches (p. 30).

Some study results, particularly on adolescent preferences, may not be consistent with earlier studies due to differences in population (mentally normal vs. dually diagnosed) and context-dependent preferences (p. 32).
There is a general need for more research concerning evidence-based design and user input into the design process across all themes (p. 35).
minimum_safe_summary: This systematic review synthesizes literature on the effects of architectural design in mental health facilities on users. Key findings indicate that therapeutic design, incorporating elements like natural light, access to gardens, and clear spatial organization, positively impacts patient and staff well-being, reduces stress, and can decrease length of stay. Specific design considerations for security, privacy, and therapeutic milieu are highlighted, emphasizing the importance of patient-centered approaches and multidisciplinary collaboration. Limitations include a scarcity of evidence-based numerical data, a lack of robust post-occupancy evaluations, and challenges in conducting interdisciplinary research, underscoring the need for more rigorous studies in this field.

paper_metadata.title: Stressed Spaces: Mental Health and Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Stressed Spaces: Mental Health and Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: HERD: Health Environments Research & Design Journal
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: OBJECTIVE: To present a comprehensive review of the research literature on the effects of the architectural designs of mental health facilities on the users. BACKGROUND: Using a team of cross-disciplinary researchers, this review builds upon previous reviews on general and geriatric healthcare design in order to focus on research undertaken for mental health care facility design. METHODS: Sources were gathered in 2010 and 2011. In 2010 a broad search was undertaken across health and architecture; in 2011, using keywords and 13 databases, researchers conducted a systematic search of peer reviewed literature addressing mental health care and architectural design published between 2005 to 2012, as well as a systematic search for academic theses for the period 2000 to 2012. Recurrent themes and subthemes were identified and numerical data that emerged from quantitative studies was tabulated. RESULTS: Key themes that emerged were nursing stations, light, therapeutic milieu, security, privacy, designing for the adolescent, forensic facilities, interior detail, patients' rooms, art, dementia, model of care, gardens, post-occupancy evaluation, and user engagement in design process. Of the 165 articles (including conference proceedings, books, and theses), 25 contained numerical data from empirical studies and 7 were review articles. CONCLUSIONS: Based on the review results, especially the growing evidence of the benefits of therapeutic design on patient and staff well-being and client length of stay, additional research questions are suggested concerning optimal design considerations, designs to be avoided, and the involvement of major stakeholders in the design process.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to certain natural or restorative environments can reduce physiological and psychological stress, impacting mental health outcomes.
Environments with specific characteristics (e.g., fascination, being away, extent, compatibility) can restore directed attention and alleviate mental fatigue.

mechanism_chain.description: Mechanism explaining how architectural features, particularly those related to control and privacy, influence stress and behavioral outcomes in mental health settings.

steps.from_construct: Lack of perceived control or privacy in built environment

steps.to_construct: Elevated physiological stress response (e.g., arousal, cortisol)
Negative affective states (e.g., anxiety, irritability, frustration)
Increased risk of maladaptive behaviors (e.g., aggression, withdrawal, safety issues)
